subject: Chemistry
topic: Why transition metals have high melting points
title: Why Transition Metals Have High Melting Points
summary: In transition metals the (n−1)d electrons join the ns electrons in metallic bonding, so the bonds are strong and the metals are hard with high melting points. Across the 3d series melting points peak near the middle (Mn is an exception) and fall to zinc (d¹⁰).

notes.title: 04 – Why Transition Metals Have High Melting Points

keyPoints: **Metallic bonding**: positive ions held together by a sea of electrons.
In transition metals, **(n−1)d electrons join the ns electrons** in bonding → stronger bonds → **high melting points**, hardness, low volatility.
3d series: melting points **peak near the middle** (V, Cr); **Mn** is anomalously low.
**Zn, Cd, Hg** (d¹⁰) melt low; mercury is a liquid.

blocks.p: The rise follows the growing number of unpaired d electrons available for bonding (up to about d⁵); after that electrons pair up and the melting points fall.
Zinc (420 °C), cadmium (321 °C) and mercury (−39 °C) have a full d¹⁰ subshell, so their metallic bonding is weak. Mercury is a liquid at room temperature.
